0.title: Waiting for His Son from Heaven
0.overview:
First Thessalonians is probably the earliest of Paul’s letters preserved in the New Testament — penned from Corinth around AD 50–51, within just weeks or months of his departure from the Thessalonian church. It is a letter warm with affection, urgent with concern, and radiant with hope. More than almost any other letter in the Pauline corpus, it vibrates with the pulse of a young church under pressure and a pastor who loves them like a father, a mother, and a brother all at once.

The city of Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia — a major port, a commercial hub, a city full of every religion Rome and the East could offer. Paul had arrived there on his second missionary journey, preached for perhaps three weeks in the synagogue, and watched as a community of faith was born — Jewish converts, god-fearing Greeks, and not a few prominent women (Acts 17:1–9). Then a riot broke out, the city authorities were alarmed, and Paul was smuggled out by night. He never forgot those he had left behind.

The letter's great themes weave together like threads in a tapestry. There is the gospel — how it arrived in Thessalonica not merely as words but in power, in the Holy Spirit, in full conviction (1:5). There is the church as a community shaped by faith, hope, and love — Paul's great triad appears here earlier than in 1 Corinthians 13. There is holiness — the call to sanctification, especially in the realm of sexual purity, that flies directly in the face of Greco-Roman culture. And there is the return of Christ — the parousia — which dominates the last two chapters and gives the whole letter its eschatological urgency. The Thessalonians were grieving for those who had died before Jesus returned; Paul's answer is the most vivid description of the Second Coming in all of Scripture.

Above all, this is a letter about hope. Not the vague optimism the world calls hope, but the taut, muscular, resurrection-grounded hope that transforms how believers grieve, how they work, how they treat their bodies, and how they face the future. 'We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep,' Paul writes, 'so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope' (4:13). That contrast — hope versus hopelessness — is the heartbeat of 1 Thessalonians. The God who raised Jesus will raise them. The Lord who ascended will descend. The church that suffers now will be presented blameless before him at his coming.

1.title: The Gospel That Works
1.overview:
This is probably the earliest letter in the New Testament, written around AD 50 from Corinth. Paul had preached in Thessalonica, capital of Macedonia, for only a few weeks before a riot forced him out by night (Acts 17:1–10). He had been frantic about the young church he left behind, and chapter 1 is his relief and thanksgiving at the news that they are standing.

He thanks God for their faith that works, love that labours and hope that endures. He knows God chose them, because the gospel came to them with the Spirit’s power and changed them. They received it with joy in the middle of persecution, and the story of their conversion has spread across Greece: they turned from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, who rescues us from the coming wrath. Turned, serving, waiting: the whole Christian life in ten verses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy write to the church of the Thessalonians, which is in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace and peace to you.
verseByVerse.theology:
Joining the Father and the Lord Jesus as a single source of grace and peace is a compressed Christology, and its date is what makes it startling. This letter is very likely the earliest document in the New Testament, written around twenty years after the crucifixion — well before any Gospel. There was no long development during which a human teacher was gradually elevated to divine status. The highest view of Christ is already here, in the first line of the first thing written, stated as though it needed no defence.

The Reformed tradition, with Nicaea, has always insisted that a creature cannot be a co-source of divine blessing. Grace and peace come from God; if they come from Jesus in the same breath and under the same preposition, then Jesus is not on the creature side of the line. The greeting is a doxology in miniature: two persons, one blessing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In Thessalonica, kyrios was Caesar's title, and the city was proud of its standing with Rome — a free city that had backed the winning side and kept its own assembly for it. Acts records the charge laid against these believers exactly: they say there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). To receive a letter greeting them from the Lord Jesus was to be reminded whose throne their welfare actually came from.

Now: Notice what Paul does not put in his greeting. No title, no credentials, no reminder of what he had done for them. Where he was loved and trusted he simply used his name. It is a small thing, and it is a fair question for anyone who holds office in a church: how much of your authority do you find you have to keep asserting, and why?

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, Silvanus and Timothy write to the church of the Thessalonians, which belongs to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace and peace to you.

How young this church was. Paul came from Philippi, where he had been beaten and jailed (Acts 16:22–24), and preached in the synagogue on three Sabbaths (Acts 17:2). Within weeks a mob dragged his host Jason before the magistrates, and the believers sent Paul away by night (Acts 17:5–10). Then they were on their own.

The earliest letter. Written a few months later from Corinth, probably before any other New Testament book.

No title. Paul does not call himself an apostle. Where his authority was challenged (Galatians 1:1), he insisted on it. Where he was loved and trusted, he simply used his name.

The team. Silvanus is the Silas who sang with Paul in the stocks at Philippi (Acts 16:25); Timothy will be sent back alone (3:2).

In God. Not “at Thessalonica”, as though the city defined them. A few dozen weeks-old converts are told where they really live.

Father and Lord together. Both under one preposition, without explanation. A Jew raised on the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) does not do that casually. Within twenty years of the cross, Jesus already stands on the divine side of the line. In a city where kyrios was Caesar’s title, believers had been accused of saying “there is another king, Jesus” (Acts 17:7).

Grace and peace. Always in that order: grace comes down; peace is what it makes when it lands.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts lengthen the greeting to “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (KJV), matching Paul’s other letters. The short form is earlier.

On a Tuesday. Leaders: how much of your authority do you find you have to keep asserting?
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the Via Egnatia, Rome’s great east–west road. Paul founded the church on his second journey but was soon driven out. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. Paul probably wrote from Corinth around AD 50, making this one of his earliest letters.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:2–10 – Faith, Love, Hope — and a Church Everyone Was Talking About
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul always thanks God for all of them, remembering their work produced by faith, labour prompted by love, and endurance inspired by hope in the Lord Jesus. He knows God chose them, because the gospel came not only in words but with power, the Holy Spirit and deep conviction, and they saw how Paul and his companions lived. They imitated them and the Lord, welcoming the message with the Spirit’s joy despite severe suffering, and became a model for believers across Macedonia and Achaia. The Lord’s message rang out from them everywhere, so that people report how they turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, whom he raised from the dead and who rescues us from the coming wrath.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and How Anyone Could Know

Verse 4 states election flatly and warmly, and verse 5 gives the grounds. Paul claims no private glimpse of the eternal register. He reasons from effect to cause: the gospel arrived among these people with power, the Spirit, and settled conviction, and it produced work, labour and endurance — therefore God had chosen them. The hidden decree becomes visible in time through the effectual call. Peter puts the order exactly: we make our calling and election sure (2 Pet. 1:10) — the election is known through the calling.

Two guards keep this from going wrong. Their faith and love are not the ground of their election — that lies wholly in God — but they are the evidence of it; fruit confirming a root nobody can dig up and inspect. And notice the pastoral use Paul makes of the doctrine. He does not deploy it to sort the congregation or to threaten. He hands it to persecuted people as the one piece of ground that cannot shift: if your standing rested on the firmness of your own decision, a hard enough season could undo it; resting on his choice, it cannot.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Thessalonica was the provincial capital, and its religion was civic rather than private. Trade guilds met at sacrificial meals under patron gods; households kept their own deities; loyalty to Rome was expressed in the imperial cult. To turn from idols was not a change of opinion but resignation from the life of the town, which is precisely why affliction followed (v.6). And the whole thing happened fast: Paul had perhaps a month in the city (Acts 17:2) before a mob forced him out at night, yet within months this church was the pattern held up to older congregations across two provinces.

Now: Verse 3 supplies a test worth running, because faith, love and hope cost nothing to claim. Paul measures each by its output — work, exhaustion, staying put. Ask not whether you have them but whether anything in your week would look different if you did not. And verse 9 gives the useful form of the idol question: since ours are rarely carved, asking whether you own any statues settles nothing. Ask what you serve — what the week is organised around, what you are most afraid of losing, what you would trade sleep and integrity to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We always thank God for all of you and continually mention you in our prayers.

Always. Paul had left in the worst way and spent months half convinced his work was wasted (3:5). Thanksgiving was not his obvious response; it was his settled one.

All. Not just the promising ones.

Constantly. Adialeiptōs, without a gap. Paul uses it three times in this short letter (1:2; 2:13; 5:17). A habit, not a mood.

What to do with worry. Paul was worried sick and could not reach them. He turned the worry into thanks and intercession, without waiting for good news (Philippians 4:6).

On a Tuesday. Name the people you are anxious about, and thank God for one specific grace in each before you ask for anything.

verseByVerse.quote: remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We remember before our God and Father the work your faith produces, the hard labour your love prompts, and the endurance your hope in our Lord Jesus Christ gives you.

The triad. Faith, love, hope, probably written down here for the first time (later 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:13). But the other nouns do the work.

Work of faith. Not work that earns salvation (Romans 4:5), but work faith produces, as a live root pushes up a shoot (Galatians 5:6; James 2:17).

Labour of love. Kopos, toil to exhaustion. Love produces the tiredness of doing something hard for someone else. Most real love in a church looks like being worn out by people.

Steadfastness of hope. Hypomonē, staying under a weight without buckling. Hope feeds endurance: you can bear almost anything if you know it ends and how (Romans 8:24–25).

In our Lord Jesus Christ. Not admirable human qualities, but what Christ produces in people joined to him.

On a Tuesday. Faith, love and hope cost nothing to claim. Would anything in your week look different without them?
verseByVerse.note: Faith, love and hope — the triad Paul returns to again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know, brothers and sisters loved by God, that he has chosen you.

Loved. A perfect passive participle: having been loved, and standing loved. A settled state, not God’s mood on a good day.

Chosen. Eklogē, election, stated plainly to a six-month-old church under persecution, as comfort. If your standing rested on your own decision, a bad enough month could undo it. Resting on God’s choice, it cannot.

How could Paul know? No one has read the eternal register. Paul gives his evidence in the next word, “because” (v. 5): the way the gospel arrived and changed them. The root is hidden; the fruit is not (2 Peter 1:10).

Views. Arminian Christians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But Paul reasons from their reception of the gospel in power and the Holy Spirit to God’s prior choice: their faith is the evidence of election, not its cause (Ephesians 1:4–5; 2:8).

How not to use it. Paul does not use election to sort the congregation or to threaten. He uses it like a title deed shown to a nervous tenant: this is yours, and here is why nobody can take it.

For the anxious. Do not try to read God’s mind. Look at the effects: a word that landed, a life that turned, a love you did not have before. Then thank him.

verseByVerse.quote: because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our gospel came to you not only in words but also with power, with the Holy Spirit, and with deep conviction. You know how we lived among you for your sake.

Not only in word. The word was necessary; there is no gospel without it (Romans 10:14). But words are the instrument, not the agent. The same sermon can leave one room unmoved and another in tears.

Power and the Spirit. Paul refuses to credit the result to his delivery (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).

Full conviction. Plērophoria: carried all the way, settled certainty. Not that they found the argument persuasive, but that it landed with the weight of fact. Probably both the preachers’ conviction and the hearers’.

What kind of men. The half often skipped. They had seen men with backs still marked from Philippi (2:2), working night and day so as not to burden anyone (2:9), leaving by night rather than endanger converts.

Both halves. The Spirit gives power; a life gives credibility. A blameless life without the word saves nobody; the word from a contradicting life is rightly dismissed.

On a Tuesday. Pray before you speak about Christ, and live so that your life does not contradict what you say.

verseByVerse.quote: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You became imitators of us and of the Lord, because in spite of severe suffering you welcomed the message with the joy given by the Holy Spirit. And so you became a model to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia.

Imitators in what? Paul says exactly: receiving the word in affliction with joy. Not his gifts or knowledge, but the way he took a beating and kept his joy (Acts 16:25).

How imitation works. They had watched him under pressure. When their turn came, they did what he did.

Much affliction. Thlipsis, crushing pressure: the mob, social exclusion, losing their place in the town (Acts 17:5–9; 2:14).

The Spirit’s joy. Not worked up, and not the absence of pain (Galatians 5:22).

The combination. Affliction without joy is misfortune; joy without affliction proves nothing. Joy inside affliction demands an explanation, and people go looking for one.

Example. Typos, the mark left by a blow: they were struck by the gospel and carried its impression.

Macedonia and Achaia. Northern and southern Greece, including Athens and Corinth. Weeks-old converts became the pattern for older churches. Time in the faith and usefulness to God are different measurements.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.

verseByVerse.quote: For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s message rang out from you, not only in Macedonia and Achaia; your faith in God has become known everywhere. So we do not need to say anything about it.

Sounded forth. Exēchētai, behind our “echo”: a trumpet blast, thunder rolling. The gospel struck this church like a hammer on a bell.

Still sounding. A perfect tense: it rang out and still rings.

Why it spread. Thessalonica sat on the Via Egnatia, Rome’s road across Greece, and was a busy port. Travellers carried the story. The church organised nothing; they lived in a city everyone passed through.

Need not say anything. Paul, whose job was talking, finds people telling him about the Thessalonians first, and is delighted to be redundant.

What travelled. Not a programme, but a report: people who dropped their idols and stayed glad under pressure.

On a Tuesday. Every church has a reputation in its town, and it is not the one on the noticeboard. What are your neighbours saying about yours?

verseByVerse.quote: For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
People everywhere report how you welcomed us, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.

Two movements. A turning to and a turning from (compare Acts 14:15; 26:18).

To God from idols. Note the order. People rarely drop an idol because it has been proved worthless in the abstract. They drop it because something better has taken hold. Reverse it, and you get willpower, a short-lived fuel.

The cost. Thessalonica was full of the worship of Dionysus, Serapis and the Cabiri, and the imperial cult. Religion was civic: trade guilds met at sacrificial meals, homes kept household gods, loyalty meant attendance. Turning from idols meant resigning from the life of the town. Hence the affliction of v. 6. And it shows most of the church were converted pagans.

Living and true. Idols are not alive (Isaiah 44:14–17: half the log for the fire, half for the god) and not true. Jeremiah: “the LORD is the true God; he is the living God” (Jeremiah 10:10).

Serve. Douleuein, serve as a slave. They did not exchange servitude for independence; they changed owners, and the new one is alive (Romans 6:17–18).

On a Tuesday. Our idols are rarely carved. Ask what you serve: what your week is organised around, what you fear losing, what you would sacrifice sleep and integrity to keep.
verseByVerse.note: Turning “from idols” shows that most of the church were converted pagans, not Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they report how you are waiting for his Son from heaven, Jesus, whom God raised from the dead and who rescues us from the coming wrath.

Serve and wait. Both present and continuous. Work and watch; neither without the other.

Wait. Expectantly, watching the road. Within weeks of conversion they had learned to live with eyes on the horizon, so much that they worried about believers who died first (4:13).

Whom he raised. The return rests on something already done in public. A man who has been raised can come back (Acts 17:31).

Wrath. Not divine temper, but God’s settled, just opposition to evil. A God indifferent to cruelty would not be good; we would not admire a judge who shrugged at atrocity (Romans 1:18; 2:5).

Delivers. Present tense: a rescue already in force. Paul tells frightened believers that wrath is not coming for them (5:9). Jesus absorbed it himself (Romans 5:9; Galatians 3:13).

What it does not mean. Not a promise that believers escape persecution or suffering; they were suffering as he wrote. It is rescue from God’s final judgment.

For worship. Turned, serving, waiting: past, present and future, all held by Jesus.

2.title: A Nursing Mother and a Urging Father
2.overview:
After Paul’s hurried departure, someone was evidently saying he had been just another travelling religious salesman: a flatterer after money and fame who ran when it got hard. Paul answers by appealing to what the Thessalonians saw with their own eyes. He came still bruised from Philippi and preached anyway. He did not flatter, cheat or seek praise, though as an apostle he could have demanded support. He was gentle as a nursing mother and urged them on like a father, and he worked night and day at his trade so as not to burden anyone.

He thanks God that they received his message as what it really is, God’s word, which is now at work in them, even though it brought persecution from their own countrymen, as the Judean churches suffered from theirs. Then his grief shows: he was “orphaned” from them, Satan blocked his return, yet they are his hope, joy and crown when the Lord Jesus comes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You know our visit was not wasted. Though we had just been mistreated at Philippi, God gave us courage to preach to you in the face of strong opposition. Our appeal did not come from error, impure motives or trickery. God approved us and entrusted us with the gospel, so we speak to please God, who tests our hearts, not people. We never used flattery or covered up greed, nor sought praise, though as apostles we could have made demands. We were gentle like a nursing mother caring for her children, and loved you so much we shared our very lives. We worked night and day so as not to be a burden while we preached. You and God are witnesses that we lived in a holy, righteous and blameless way. Like a father with his children, we urged, encouraged and pleaded with each of you to live lives worthy of God, who calls you into his kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Minister as Steward, Not Owner

The governing idea of the passage is in verse 4: entrusted with the gospel. The word is used of a deposit placed in someone's keeping. It is not Paul's gospel, as though he had devised it — he is a courier carrying what belongs to another, and a courier does not edit the parcel. The Reformed tradition has always insisted the minister stands under the word rather than over it: a steward, never an entrepreneur.

Notice that Paul uses the assayer's word dokimazo twice in one sentence. He has been tested and approved; and he speaks before the God who goes on testing hearts. The examination is continuous, which is why the sentence lands where it does — not to please man, but to please God. This is not indifference to people; Paul has just described treating them with a nursing mother's tenderness. It is a question of whose verdict he is working for, and the two audiences pull apart at exactly the point where the true thing and the popular thing separate.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The circuit Paul travelled was worked by professional lecturers and religious salesmen who lived on their rhetoric, took what they could get, and moved on. The quickest way to destroy a young church was to persuade it that its founder had been one of them. So Paul answers with what could be checked: they had watched him arrive injured and preach anyway, and they had watched him at a leatherworker's bench before dawn and after dark so that none of them would have to pay for him.

Now: Verse 6 is the sharpest line for anyone holding office. Paul had the right to be supported and honoured, defends that right vigorously elsewhere (1 Cor 9:4-14), and declined to press it. The question in ministry — as in any relationship where one party holds the power — is almost never whether you have a right. Usually you do. It is what you intend to do with it. And verse 9 needs its guard: Paul is not ruling out paid ministry, which he explicitly upholds (1 Cor 9:14; and 5:12 below). He waived a fair claim in one place for one reason, so that nothing about money could stand between these people and the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves know, brothers and sisters, that our visit to you was not a failure. Although we had just suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, as you know, our God gave us courage to tell you his gospel in spite of strong opposition.

The accusation. You can hear it in what Paul denies: a flatterer, after money, chasing reputation, who ran off. Travelling philosophers and religious salesmen worked that road constantly. The quickest way to destroy a young church was to say its founder was one of them.

You know. Four times in twelve verses (vv. 1, 2, 5, 11). His defence is their memory.

Not in vain. Kenos, empty. The church reading the letter was the proof.

Philippi. Stripped in the market, beaten with rods, put in the stocks, though Roman citizens (Acts 16:22–24, 37). “Shamefully treated” means insult as well as injury. Thessalonica was a hundred miles on. He arrived still marked.

Boldness in our God. Parrhēsia, free and open speech, sourced not in his nerve but in God. Borrowed courage (Acts 4:29–31).

Much conflict. Agōn, the arena struggle, going on while he spoke. It ended in a riot (Acts 17:5).

The cost is the credential. A man in it for money does not walk from a flogging into a riot.

On a Tuesday. When you are afraid to speak of Christ, ask God for borrowed boldness. He gives it.
verseByVerse.note: At Philippi Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed just before they came to Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our appeal does not come from error, impure motives or trickery. Rather, God has approved us and entrusted us with the gospel, so we speak, not to please people, but to please God, who tests our hearts.

Three ways ministry goes wrong. Error (planē): wrong message, sincerely held. Impurity (akatharsia): wrong motive, often sexual; travelling teachers with access to households were a known hazard. Deceit (dolos): wrong method, a word used for baiting a hook. Any one ruins a ministry sound in the other two.

Approved. Dokimazō, the assayer testing metal, used twice: tested and passed, by a God who keeps testing.

Entrusted. A deposit in someone’s keeping. Not Paul’s gospel; he is a courier, and a courier does not edit the parcel (Galatians 1:10–12).

Not to please man. Not indifference to people; he was tender with them (v. 7). A question of whose verdict he works for. The audiences part company exactly where the true thing and the popular thing separate.

On a Tuesday. Parents, teachers, preachers: in the moment when truth and popularity divide, which approval do you reach for?

verseByVerse.quote: For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We never used flattery, as you know, nor did we put on a mask to cover up greed; God is our witness. We were not looking for praise from people, from you or anyone else, even though as apostles of Christ we could have asserted our authority.

Flattery. Not kindness, but praise with a hook in it. Ancient moralists despised the flatterer as a manipulator in a friend’s face. For this, Paul appeals to their memory.

A pretext for greed. A cover story: ministry as a front for profit. Motives are invisible, so here Paul calls a different witness: God.

Glory from people. Subtler than money and more common among religious people. A man can be scrupulous about cash and still feed on admiration. “Or from others”: he was not building a reputation to spend elsewhere.

Could have made demands. He had the right to support and honour, and defends it elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:4–14), then declines to use it.

The mind of Christ. Who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6).

On a Tuesday. In any relationship where you hold power, the question is rarely whether you have a right. It is what you will do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her own children. We loved you so much that we were glad to share with you not only the gospel of God but our very lives, because you had become so dear to us.

A nursing mother. Trophos, with “her own”: not a hired wet-nurse but a mother feeding her own child, at night, unseen, unthanked. An image no one expected from Paul.

A textual note. Manuscripts divide between ēpioi, “gentle”, and nēpioi, “infants”, one letter apart, and the previous word ends in that letter. The earliest copies favour “infants” (“we became little children among you”), but the sudden switch to a nursing mother makes “gentle” the smoother sense, which the ESV adopts. Either way, the charge of self-importance collapses.

Affectionately desirous. Homeiromenoi, found only here in the New Testament; on a gravestone it describes parents longing for a lost child.

Our own selves. The gospel was the errand; himself was thrown in. It is possible to deliver the message accurately and withhold the person: correct content, carefully rationed distance.

Very dear. Not a strategy. He had grown to love them.

On a Tuesday. Everyone knows the difference between being served by someone who likes them and by someone doing a duty. Give yourself, not just your help.

verseByVerse.quote: For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You remember, brothers and sisters, our hard work and toil. We worked night and day so as not to be a burden to anyone while we preached the gospel of God to you.

Labour and toil. Kopos and mochthos: exhaustion and grind. Paul describes being tired.

The trade. Tentmaking or leatherwork (Acts 18:3): heavy work with awl and knife, the kind gentlemen despised. A status-seeking philosopher did not sit in a workshop.

Night and day. At the bench before dawn and after dark, preaching fitted round it. He also received gifts from Philippi (Philippians 4:16), but not from them.

Not a burden. He had the right (v. 6) and paid out of his own pocket instead.

The answer without argument. They had watched him come to meetings with workshop-stained hands.

What it does not mean. Not that ministers should be unpaid; Paul argues the opposite (1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18; and 5:12 here). He waived a right so money could not stand between them and the gospel.

On a Tuesday. Be willing to be out of pocket rather than let a fair claim of yours block someone else’s faith.
verseByVerse.note: Paul supported himself by his trade — he was a tentmaker.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous and blameless we were among you who believe. You know that we dealt with each of you as a father deals with his own children, encouraging, comforting and urging you to live lives worthy of God, who calls you into his kingdom and glory.

Both courts. Theirs saw his conduct; God’s sees his heart.

Holy, righteous, blameless. Towards God, towards people, and with nothing chargeable. Not sinlessness, but no accusation that would stick.

Like a father. After the mother (v. 7): the one responsible in the ancient household for what a child became.

Three verbs. Exhort (come alongside), encourage (put heart in), charge (put under solemn obligation). A father who only encourages raises children who cannot stand; one who only charges raises children who leave.

Each one. In a month, working night and day, he dealt with them individually.

Worthy of God. Not a standard to earn, but conduct that fits what has happened to you, like a uniform fits the service (Ephesians 4:1).

Calls. Present tense: still calling them towards kingdom and glory. Paul’s motivation is not “behave, or else” but “this is where you are going; live like it”.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “called” (past). The present is better attested.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:13–16 – How They Received the Word — and What It Cost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul constantly thanks God that when they heard the message, they accepted it not as human words but as what it truly is, the word of God, which is at work in those who believe. They became imitators of the Judean churches, suffering from their own countrymen as those churches did from their opponents, who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, drove Paul out, displease God and oppose everyone by trying to stop the gospel reaching the Gentiles. So they keep filling up their sins, and wrath has come upon them at last.
verseByVerse.theology:
Scripture as God's Own Speech

Verse 13 is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament of what Scripture is: received as human opinion the word does nothing; received as what it really is, the word of God, it goes to work (energeitai). Paul is describing not two kinds of Bible but two kinds of hearing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 15–16 have been misused across the centuries. Paul, a Jew who insists God has not rejected his people (Rom 9:3; 11:1), names a target by its actions — those who killed Jesus and the prophets and were blocking the mission to the Gentiles — in the insider language of covenant rebuke.

Now: The wrath of verse 16 must be read beside 1:10, where wrath is what Jesus delivers people from — Paul himself included. A sober warning is never a licence for contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We also constantly thank God that when you received the word of God you heard from us, you accepted it not as a human word, but as it actually is, the word of God, which is at work in you who believe.

Received and accepted. Paralambanō, taking delivery; dechomai, welcoming as a guest. Hearing, then embracing. Many do the first every Sunday and never the second.

As it really is. They heard it from a scarred leatherworker in a rented room in a city full of lecturers. Nothing about the delivery compelled the verdict. They concluded God was addressing them.

The choice every reader makes. If the Bible is a valuable human document, you weigh it and keep what persuades you: you remain judge. If it is God’s word, it reads you. There is no option where it is God’s word and you hold the editor’s pencil.

At work. Energeitai, present and continuous. The word did not inform them once; it is working now (Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 55:11).

Two kinds of hearing. Received as opinion, the word does nothing. Received as God’s word, it produces the faith, love and endurance of 1:3.

On a Tuesday. Before you open your Bible, pray: “Speak, for your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10).

verseByVerse.quote: For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of God’s churches in Judea that are in Christ Jesus. You suffered from your own people the same things those churches suffered from theirs.

Imitators again. In 1:6, of Paul and the Lord; here, of churches far away they had never met.

Your own countrymen. Judean believers were opposed by fellow Jews; Thessalonian believers by fellow Greeks (Acts 17:5–9). Opposition from neighbours hurts most: the loss of your own people.

What it meant. They had walked out of guild dinners, household shrines and civic festivals. Pressure came from employers, families and lifelong friends.

The pastoral point. A young church asks at night: has something gone wrong? Paul: you have joined a line, the oldest churches in the faith. Suffering is not evidence of a wrong turn (John 15:20; 2 Timothy 3:12).

What it does not mean. Opposition does not prove faithfulness; some people are disliked for being disagreeable. Nor does it prove failure.

On a Tuesday. If your family opposes your faith, you are not alone. Pray for them, and stay kind.

verseByVerse.quote: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!
verseByVerse.commentary:
They killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and drove us out. They displease God and are hostile to everyone, trying to keep us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved. In this way they keep filling up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last.

Misused for centuries. This passage has been used to justify terrible things. Its limits must be stated plainly.

Who speaks. Paul was a Jew, “a Hebrew of Hebrews” (Philippians 3:5), who wished himself accursed for his kinsmen and insisted God has not rejected his people (Romans 9:3; 11:1). Whatever this means, it cannot mean what Romans denies.

Who is meant. Not a race, but those named by their actions: authorities who killed Jesus and the prophets, drove the missionaries out, and were blocking the gospel from reaching Gentiles (Acts 17:5, 13). Paul himself had once done the same (Galatians 1:13).

Insider rebuke. The prophets said harder things about Israel’s leaders; Jesus wept over Jerusalem for killing the prophets (Matthew 23:37). This is covenant rebuke from within. It becomes something else when outsiders use it as a weapon.

Oppose all mankind. By blocking the one message that saves. A charge about the mission, not about character.

Wrath has come. A prophetic past tense: judgment so certain it can be spoken of as arrived. Within twenty years Jerusalem fell.

Added later? Some scholars think vv. 13–16 were inserted after AD 70. No manuscript lacks them, and they fit Paul’s experience (Acts 17:5, 13).

A textual note. Many later manuscripts read “their own prophets” (KJV). The shorter “the prophets” is earlier.

The guard. Wrath is what Jesus delivers from (1:10), including Paul, a former persecutor. The same gospel stands open to all. Anyone who uses this passage for contempt has read the man who wrote Romans 11 exactly backwards.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, as he had once done — not of every Jewish person.

parallels.desc: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete

verseByVerse.ref: 2:17–20 – Orphaned From Them, and What He Expects to Hold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Torn away from them for a short time, in body but not in heart, Paul longed intensely to see them face to face. He wanted to come, again and again, but Satan blocked the way. For what is his hope, joy and crown of boasting when the Lord Jesus comes? Is it not them? They are his glory and joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Coming, and the Pastor's Wreath

Verse 19 brings in parousia, the word for a sovereign's state visit, and pictures Paul at the King's arrival holding nothing but a wreath made of people. The reward of pastoral work is not the admiration of the present age but the sight, on that day, of people standing before Jesus because the gospel was faithfully preached and patiently tended.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul read his blocked return not as bad luck or as God saying no but as the work of an enemy — and the enemy did not win: Timothy went in his place, and this letter exists because Paul could not come.

Now: On the last day, is what you expect to hold up a record of what you achieved, or people who are standing there because of it?

verseByVerse.quote: But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face, because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But, brothers and sisters, when we were separated from you for a short time, in person though not in thought, we made every effort to see you, because we longed to. We wanted to come to you, I, Paul, more than once, but Satan stopped us.

Orphaned. Aporphanisthentes, from the word for orphan. Having called himself their mother and father, he is now the bereaved parent.

For a short time; not in heart. Temporary, and only physical.

More eagerly. Separation made him try harder, not settle.

I, Paul. The sentence breaks; he drops the plural to sign his name: I tried, again and again.

Hindered. Enekopsen, to cut into a road to stop an army.

How? We do not know. Perhaps the bond the magistrates took from Jason (Acts 17:9), making Paul’s return dangerous for his hosts; perhaps illness or other hostility.

Can Satan thwart God? He can hinder our plans, but only within God’s permission (Job 1–2; 2 Corinthians 12:7). God used even this: Timothy went (3:2), and this letter exists because Paul could not come.

Balance. Not every delay is demonic; reading every setback so leads to exhaustion and superstition. But Paul did not think his frustrations merely administrative.

On a Tuesday. When good plans are blocked, pray against the enemy and trust the Lord who turns even blocked roads into letters.

verseByVerse.quote: For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what is our hope, our joy, or the crown we will boast in before our Lord Jesus when he comes? Is it not you? Indeed, you are our glory and joy.

What he is after. Accused of chasing glory (v. 6), he names his real glory: them.

Crown. Stephanos, the victor’s wreath, also placed on dignitaries honoured when a ruler visited a city.

His coming. Parousia, first used here: a sovereign’s state visit, citizens streaming out to meet him and escort him in. Paul applies it to Jesus’ return (4:15–17).

The picture. The King arrives, and what Paul holds is not a record of his labours but a group of people. They are the wreath (Philippians 4:1).

Are. Present tense: now, while separated.

The real answer to the charge. A glory-seeker uses people and moves on. Paul’s glory is them.

On a Tuesday. On the last day, do you expect to hold up a record of achievement, or people who are standing there because of you? Invest in people.

3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview:
Paul could not bear not knowing whether the young church had survived persecution. So he stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy back to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was what they had been warned to expect, and fearing that the tempter had talked them out of the faith. Now Timothy has returned with good news: their faith and love are holding, and they long to see Paul as he longs to see them.

Paul says, “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.” He cannot thank God enough, and prays night and day to see them and fill the gaps in their teaching. The chapter ends with a prayer that God will clear his road to them, make their love overflow to everyone, and strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness when Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Paul could stand it no longer, he chose to be left alone in Athens and sent Timothy, his brother and God’s co-worker, to strengthen and encourage them, so that no one would be unsettled by their troubles. They knew they were destined for this; Paul had told them in advance they would suffer, and so it happened. Unable to bear it, he sent to find out about their faith, afraid the tempter had tempted them and his work had been wasted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as Appointment, Not Accident

The key word in verse 3 is keimetha — we are laid, set in place, appointed. It is the language of a stone set in a foundation or a sentry posted, and Paul uses the same root of himself in prison, put there for the defence of the gospel (Phil 1:16). Suffering for the gospel is not something that slipped past God's attention; it is a placement.

That is the pastoral logic, and it needs stating carefully. What steadies a shaken believer is not the promise that the trouble will stop but the assurance that the trouble is not a mistake. If hardship means the plan has gone wrong, every difficult week is evidence against the faith. If hardship is where God has laid you, the difficult week proves only that you are where he put you. The Reformed tradition has held this consistently: God governs all things, his people's afflictions included, and such suffering is purposeful — producing endurance, character and hope (Rom 5:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them out of it (v.3) — faith is usually lost by erosion, not by renunciation.

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and its absence is a cruelty disguised as encouragement (v.4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when we could stand it no longer, we decided to be left alone in Athens, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s co-worker in spreading the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith.

Could bear it no longer. Stegō, to hold water out, as a roof or a watertight jar. Paul had been holding in his anxiety, and the seams gave way. He says it twice (vv. 1, 5).

Alone at Athens. The city where Paul was provoked by idols, mocked at the mention of resurrection, and made few converts (Acts 17:16–34): his thinnest ground. There, he gave away his companion. “Alone” stands last in the Greek, with weight. He chose isolation because a frightened church needed someone more than he did. That is 2:8, sharing “our own selves”, as an actual decision.

The sequence. Acts 17:14–15 has Silas and Timothy staying in Macedonia while Paul went on; they evidently rejoined him at Athens, then Timothy was sent back, and both met Paul again at Corinth (Acts 18:5).

God’s co-worker. Not “my assistant”. Steadying a church is God’s work, and Timothy works alongside God (1 Corinthians 3:9).

A textual note. Manuscripts vary: “God’s co-worker”, “minister of God”, or both combined. Scribes may have softened the bold “co-worker of God”. The ESV reading is probably original.

Establish and exhort. To prop a leaning wall, and to come alongside and urge. Under attack, the first task is not growth but keeping the church standing.

On a Tuesday. Whose need is greater than your comfort this week? Send help, even if it costs you company.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy came so that none of you would be shaken by these troubles. You know very well that we are destined for them.

Moved. Sainesthai, first used of a dog wagging its tail: fawned on, coaxed. Paul’s fear was not that persecution would smash them but that they would be gently talked out of the faith.

How faith is usually lost. Not by dramatic renunciation, but by erosion: the family who keep asking, the invitation easier to accept, the guild dinner too costly to refuse. A wagging tail, not a battering ram (Mark 4:17).

Destined. Keimetha, “we are laid”: set in place like a foundation stone, posted like a sentry. The same root Paul uses of himself in prison: “I am put here for the defense of the gospel” (Philippians 1:16).

The pastoral logic. What steadies a shaken believer is not that the trouble will stop, but that it is not a mistake. If suffering means the plan has failed, every hard week is evidence against the faith. If it is where God has placed you, it proves only that you are where he put you (Romans 5:3–4; 1 Peter 4:12).

What it does not mean. Not that God delights in his people’s pain, or that we should seek suffering. Persecution is still evil; God rules it for good.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we were with you, we kept telling you that we would suffer persecution, and it turned out that way, as you know. That is why, when I could stand it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith. I was afraid that the tempter had tempted you and our work had been in vain.

Told beforehand. Continuous tense: he kept telling them, in a stay of a few weeks. He did not win them with an easier offer and explain the terms later (Acts 14:22).

Verified by events. When trouble came, it confirmed the teaching instead of contradicting it. A church told the truth can say “he said this would happen”; a church promised an easy road asks whether the whole thing was false.

The tempter. Satan’s title in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3), where the method was suggestion, not violence. Block the teacher (2:18), then work on the church.

In vain. Kenos, the “empty” of 2:1. The confident apostle also lay awake fearing his work had come to nothing.

Faith and anxiety. Paul was sure of God and frightened about the outcome at once. He could not go, so he sent, and waited (compare 2 Corinthians 11:28).

On a Tuesday. When you teach new believers, tell them honestly what following Christ costs. It is a kindness.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Timothy has returned with good news of their faith and love: they remember Paul fondly and long to see him, as he longs to see them. In all his own distress, their faith has comforted him. Now he truly lives, since they are standing firm in the Lord. He cannot thank God enough for the joy they bring, and prays night and day to see them and supply what is lacking in their faith. May God our Father and the Lord Jesus clear the way for him to come; may the Lord make their love for each other and for everyone grow and overflow, as his does for them; and may he strengthen their hearts to be blameless and holy before God when the Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Persons, One Verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus as two subjects and gives them one singular verb — the highest view of Christ, already present in the ordinary shape of a man's prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith (v.10) was not sincerity but completeness — the teaching Paul never got to give.

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love not only for one another but ‘for all’ (v.12) — the very population making its life hard.

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Timothy has just come back to us from you and brought good news about your faith and love. He tells us that you always have fond memories of us and long to see us, just as we long to see you. So, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and suffering we have been encouraged about you because of your faith.

The news arrives. The letter changes temperature.

Gospelled. Euangelisamenou, the verb for preaching the good news, used by Paul only here for anything other than the gospel. A church standing firm was good news of the same order.

Three fears answered. Faith: they had not been coaxed away. Love: they had not turned on one another. Remembrance: they had not concluded he abandoned them, as his enemies said.

The comforted apostle. Their faith comforts him. In Corinth he was “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3), and the Lord had to tell him in a vision not to be afraid (Acts 18:9–10).

Two-way traffic. In a healthy church the strengtheners are held up by the ordinary believers they worry about (Romans 1:12).

On a Tuesday. If you wonder whether your quiet faithfulness matters to anyone: it was what got Paul through Corinth. Tell your pastor how you are doing.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we really live, since you are standing firm in the Lord.

Alive. Not merely relieved: alive. The months of not knowing were a kind of death.

What it does not mean. Not the unhealthy dependence of a leader whose identity rests on his people’s performance. Paul sought no glory from them (2:6). This is love, and love always makes your wellbeing hostage to someone else’s (3 John 4).

Standing fast. Stēkete, a soldier holding his place in the line (Philippians 1:27; 4:1). Not advancing or achieving; still there when the pushing stopped.

In the Lord. Not by stubbornness or loyalty to Paul. The place they held was a person.

On a Tuesday. These new converts had simply not given up. They did not know that their not giving up was what an apostle was living on. Neither do you.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can we thank God enough for you, in return for all the joy we have in God’s presence because of you? Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you again and supply what is lacking in your faith.

A real question. Paul has run out of ways to say thank you.

Before our God. Joy over others is held up in God’s presence, because he did it.

Most earnestly. A double superlative: the ordinary intensifiers would not carry it. “Night and day” is the phrase of 2:9: whatever Paul did at night, he did not sleep much.

What is lacking. Not a rebuke after eight verses of praise. Katartisai means to set a bone or mend a net (Matthew 4:21): to make complete. What was lacking was the teaching he never got to give in a few weeks. Chapters 4–5 begin to supply it.

Two kinds of gap. A deficiency that is a fault, and one that is an unfinished education. Paul meets the second not with reproach but with longing to fill it.

On a Tuesday. If your faith feels patchy, ask whether nobody ever taught you. Then find a good teacher or book, and fill the gap.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may our God and Father himself and our Lord Jesus clear the way for us to come to you.

Two persons, one verb. The Father and the Lord Jesus are the subjects; the verb “direct” is singular. Paul names two and speaks of them acting as one, without explanation (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:16–17). Within twenty years of the cross, this is the ordinary shape of his prayer.

Clear the road. Kateuthynai, to make straight: against 2:18, where Satan “cut into” it. The enemy truly obstructs; the Sovereign truly governs; only one is prayed to.

Refused, for a while. So far as we know, Paul did not return for years (perhaps Acts 20:1–2). Instead came Timothy’s report and this letter, which has done more for the church than the visit could.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts add “Christ” after “Jesus”.

On a Tuesday. Pray about the blocked road, then do the work you can from where you are.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the Lord make your love for one another and for everyone else increase and overflow, just as ours does for you. May he strengthen your hearts so that you will be blameless and holy in the presence of our God and Father when our Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

A flood. “Increase and abound”: multiply and overflow the banks.

And for all. The sharp phrase. A persecuted community naturally turns inward and keeps its warmth for insiders; that is the beginning of a sect. Paul prays they will overflow with love for the very people making their life hard (Matthew 5:44).

As we do for you. Paul’s love, demonstrated in chapters 2–3, is the measure.

The Lord makes you. Not “try harder”. Ask God for what you then work at (4:9–10).

Establish. What Timothy was sent to do (v. 2), Paul now asks God to do. That is how ministry works.

Blameless in holiness. The hinge into chapter 4, which begins with holiness (4:3).

With all his saints. Most likely the angels, on the pattern of Zechariah 14:5: “the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.” Others include believers who have died (4:14). Either way, a prophet’s picture of God arriving is applied to Jesus.

A textual note. Some manuscripts end the verse with “Amen”.

For worship. Love now is how a church gets ready for then.

parallels.desc: the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone,<sup>2</sup>and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,<sup>3</sup>that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.<sup>4</sup>For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know.<sup>5</sup>For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.<sup>6</sup>But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you—<sup>7</sup>for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.<sup>8</sup>For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God,<sup>10</sup>as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?<sup>11</sup>Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,<sup>12</sup>and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you,<sup>13</sup>so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

4.title: Holy Living and the Blessed Hope
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the great hinge of 1 Thessalonians, where exhortation meets eschatology. The first half (vv. 1–12) is a call to practical holiness — above all in the realm of sexual purity — that reads like a bracing cold shower after the warmth of the first three chapters. The second half (vv. 13–18) contains the most vivid and detailed account of the Second Coming in all of Paul's letters, a passage that has consoled believers across twenty centuries of death and grief.

The connection between the two halves is not accidental. Holiness now is shaped by hope then. The God who calls the Thessalonians to sexual purity is the same God who will raise the dead. The Lord who is coming with a shout is the Lord under whose authority the body belongs. Ethics and eschatology are not separate departments of Christian thought; they interpenetrate. How you live is shaped by what you expect, and what you expect governs how you live.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–8 – The Will of God Is Your Sanctification
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from report to request, and the hinge is the prayer he has just prayed (3:13). He asks and urges rather than commands, affirms that they are already walking to please God, and asks for more of it (v.1) — reminding them that the instructions came through the Lord Jesus, not from him (v.2).

Then the content: this is the will of God, your sanctification — beginning with abstaining from sexual immorality (v.3); each one knowing how to keep his own vessel in holiness and honour (v.4), not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God (v.5); and nobody transgressing or defrauding his brother in the matter, because the Lord avenges all such things, as they had been warned in advance (v.6).

The ground is the calling itself: God did not call them for impurity but in holiness (v.7). So rejecting this rejects not a man but God — the God who goes on giving his Holy Spirit into them (v.8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body, and Who Lives In It

Paul grounds Christian sexual ethics not in his own authority or in respectability but in the Holy Spirit, whom God goes on giving into the believer (v.8). The claim on the Christian's body is not that God is restrictive but that God has moved in (cf. 1 Cor 6:19-20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Greco-Roman sexual ethics were governed by status and property; Paul brought a different account of what a person is, and applied one standard to men and women alike.

Now: Verse 6 names the victim: sexual sin is always something done to a person, and the Lord is an avenger for those who never had redress.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, then, brothers, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Finally, then' does not mean Paul is winding up — two chapters remain. It marks the turn from what he has been reporting to what he now asks, and the hinge is the prayer he has just prayed: that God would establish their hearts blameless in holiness (3:13). What follows is that prayer spelled out as instructions.

Watch the verbs he chooses. 'We ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus.' The first is the ordinary word for making a request of someone; the second is parakaleo, to come alongside and appeal. Neither is a command, and this from a man who had every right to issue one. Having already told them he would not press his apostolic rights (2:6), he now writes the way he said he behaved.

The standard is 'how you ought to walk and to please God' — and see which of those two comes first in Paul's mind. Not a rulebook but a relationship: the aim of Christian conduct is that a Person is pleased. That is a different motive from compliance, and it produces different behaviour, because you can satisfy a rule without ever thinking about the one who gave it.

Then the gracious qualification: 'just as you are doing.' Before he corrects anything he confirms that they are already on the road. He is not writing to people who have failed; he is writing to people who are doing well and asking for more. 'More and more' will come twice in this chapter (vv. 1, 10), and it is the letter's characteristic note. There is no plateau in the Christian life at which growth becomes optional.

Verse 2 carries the authority for everything that follows: 'you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.' The word is parangelias — a military term for orders passed down a chain of command. Paul has just declined to give commands in his own name; here he tells them why he does not need to. These were never his orders. They came through him from the Lord Jesus, and he was as much under them as they were.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
People often say they wish they knew the will of God for their lives. Paul states it here in a single sentence, and it is not about a job or a marriage or a city: 'this is the will of God, your sanctification.' Whatever else God may or may not disclose about your circumstances, this much is published: he intends to make you holy.

And the first application is the body. 'That you abstain from sexual immorality' — porneia, the broad word covering every sexual act outside marriage.

To feel the force of this you have to see the world it landed in. Greco-Roman sexual ethics were governed by status and property, not by any notion that the body was sacred. A married man's use of slaves, prostitutes and concubines was socially unremarkable; what was policed was another citizen's wife, because that was theft. A speech preserved under Demosthenes’ name could set out the arrangement without embarrassment: courtesans for pleasure, concubines for daily care, wives for legitimate children. Into that Paul says the body is not a piece of property governed by appetite, and that the same standard applies to men and women alike. It was not a tightening of existing morality. It was a different account of what a person is.

Verse 4 contains a genuine translation question. 'That each one of you know how to control his own skeuos' — the word means vessel or instrument. It may mean the body, and so self-control (as the ESV takes it); or it may mean a wife, and so 'know how to take a wife for himself' in holiness and honour rather than in lust. Both readings are defensible and old. What is not in doubt is the standard either way — 'in holiness and honour' — which rules out treating a person as an instrument for one's own appetite, and that is precisely what both readings forbid.

Which reading is more likely? The ESV’s body is the more likely: the context is self-control in sexual matters, and the command is given to each one of you, single and married. Either way the point is the same: sexual life is to be lived in holiness and honour.

'Not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God.' Paul draws a straight line from ignorance of God to disordered desire. He is not saying pagans were uniquely wicked; the ancient world had moralists who taught restraint. He is saying that when God is not known, there is no reason the body should be treated as anything but a means of pleasure — and that the reason a Christian treats it otherwise is not superior willpower but knowledge of God.
verseByVerse.note: To “control his own body” may instead mean “take a wife for himself”; the phrase can be read either way.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the verse that gives the passage its teeth — because it names the victim.

'That no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter.' Up to now the argument has been about holiness and the will of God. Now Paul says that sexual sin is also, always, something done to a person. The word behind 'wrong' is pleonektein, from the root meaning to have more — to overreach, to take advantage, to defraud. It is a commercial word. Paul uses it of sexual sin because that is what it is: taking from someone something that was not yours, to get more for yourself.

That cuts through a great deal of modern discussion, in which sexual behaviour between consenting adults is treated as a private matter affecting nobody. Paul's category is different. There is a brother or sister on the other side of it — the person used, the spouse betrayed, the family fractured, the future partner defrauded. Sin here is not merely impurity; it is theft from a person Christ died for.

'Because the Lord is an avenger in all these things.' Ekdikos — the one who brings justice for the wronged. Note what this implies. Sexual sin very often goes unpunished in this life and its victims frequently get no hearing at all; the powerful have generally been able to use people and keep their reputation. Paul says there is a court that does not work that way. To the person who has been wronged and never had redress, this verse is not a threat but a promise.

'As we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.' Again the honest ministry of chapter 3 — he had said all this while he was with them. He is not springing a new severity on converts who were recruited on easier terms.

And a word to anyone reading this who is on the wrong side of it, since Paul's letters are always written to actual sinners: the God who is an avenger for the wronged is the same God who, three verses earlier, is named as the one who makes people holy. The passage exists because such people can be changed. It is a warning precisely because there is a way out.

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness.' The calling determines the character. Paul does not argue from consequences or from health or from social order; he argues from what these people were summoned into. Holiness is not an advanced option for keen Christians. It is the content of the invitation.

Then verse 8, and the escalation is deliberate and startling: 'whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God.' The verb means to set aside, to reject as having no authority.

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say 'I am an apostle, so you must obey me.' He has spent chapter 2 refusing that move. He says the instruction was never his to begin with (v.2, through the Lord Jesus), so setting it aside is not a disagreement with Paul at all. There is nobody in between to argue with.

And then the ground, which is the most beautiful thing in the paragraph: God 'who gives his Holy Spirit to you.' Two details. The tense is present and continuous — not who once gave, but who goes on giving. And the preposition is into you.

So the argument for sexual holiness ends not with a threat but with a Person. The Spirit is not a force issued at conversion and then filed away; he is a Person continually given, who lives in the body under discussion. That is why this is not moralism. Paul could have made the case from purity codes or from social respectability, and he does neither. He asks them to consider who is inside them.

Paul will make the same argument at length to Corinth — your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, you are not your own, you were bought with a price (1 Cor 6:19-20). The Christian's body is not his own property to dispose of, and the reason is not that God is restrictive but that God has moved in.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:9–12 – Brotherly Love and the Quiet Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On brotherly love Paul says they need no instruction, since they are theodidaktoi — taught by God himself to love one another (v.9) — and they are doing it, right across Macedonia; but he urges them to do so more and more (v.10).

Then three instructions that belong with it: aspire to live quietly, mind your own affairs, work with your hands, as he had instructed them (v.11) — so that they may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on nobody (v.12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Covenant, Landed

Theodidaktoi appears nowhere in Greek literature before this letter; Paul seems to have coined it. He is almost certainly reaching for Jeremiah's new covenant promise — I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts, and they shall all know me, from the least to the greatest (Jer 31:33-34).

That is a considerable claim to make about a congregation of ex-pagans a few months old. Paul says the promised covenant has visibly arrived among them — and his evidence is not their doctrine but their love, which is the more striking because he was driven out before he could teach them much. What they know, God taught them from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Why would a church need telling to work? Almost certainly because of the subject of the next paragraph. If the Lord is returning imminently, why keep a trade, why plan, why save? The problem worsened rather than resolved: in the second letter Paul has to deal with people who are 'not busy at work, but busybodies', and rules that anyone unwilling to work should not eat (2 Thess 3:10-12). And 'work with your hands' was an affront to Greek sensibility — manual labour was for slaves and the poor, not for men with philosophical pretensions.

Now: The principle is one the letter keeps insisting on: expecting the Lord's return should make a Christian more reliable, not less. Idleness is treated here as a failure of love, because the idle man's food comes from somewhere and the somewhere is his brothers. Note too the ambition Paul actually commends — philotimeisthai hesychazein, make it your point of honour to be unremarkable. The New Testament's aim for most Christians is not a platform but ordinary competence: your own work done well, your own business minded, and nobody made poorer for having you around.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another, for that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul turns to philadelphia, brotherly love — and does something charming with it. 'You have no need for anyone to write to you' — and then writes to them about it anyway. It is a gracious way of raising a subject: I am not going to teach you this, because you already know it.

The reason is a word that appears nowhere else in Greek literature before this letter. They have been theodidaktoi — God-taught. Paul seems to have coined it, and he is almost certainly reaching for Jeremiah's new covenant promise: I will put my law within them, I will write it on their hearts, and they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest (Jer 31:33-34).

That is a considerable claim about a congregation of ex-pagans a few months old. Paul says the promised new covenant has visibly landed on them — not because they had excellent teaching, since he was run out of town before he could give much, but because God had written it inside them. Their love for one another is his evidence that the Spirit is at work.

And the love had travelled: 'that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia.' Not only within their own congregation but across the province — Philippi, Berea, wherever believers were. A young church under persecution, with little money, was reaching outside its own walls. That is not the natural behaviour of a frightened minority, and it is the answer to Paul's prayer a few verses earlier that they would abound in love for one another and for all (3:12).

Then, having praised them warmly, 'we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more.' The second occurrence in the chapter. Paul's pattern here repays copying by anyone who has to encourage or correct: name honestly what is already good, then ask for growth from there rather than from a deficit. He never uses praise as a softening device before the real point. The praise is the real point, and the request grows out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three instructions, and the first is almost a joke in Greek: 'aspire to live quietly.' The verb philotimeisthai means to be ambitious, to make it your point of honour — the word for a man competing for public distinction. Paul says: make it your ambition to be unremarkable. Be driven about being calm.

'Mind your own affairs' is the natural companion — attend to your own business rather than everyone else's. And 'work with your hands' is the practical outworking, and it was an affront to Greek sensibility. Manual labour was what slaves and the poor did; a man with philosophical pretensions did not sit at a bench. Paul, who had done exactly that among them night and day (2:9), tells them to do it too.

Why does this need saying? Almost certainly because of the subject of the next paragraph. If the Lord is returning imminently, some concluded, why keep working? Why plan, why save, why bother with an ordinary trade? The problem got worse rather than better — Paul has to address it far more sharply in the second letter, where some are 'not busy at work, but busybodies' and are told that if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thess 3:10-12).

So this is the first appearance of a principle the letter will keep insisting on: expecting the Lord's return should make you more reliable, not less. The person who stops working because Jesus is coming has misunderstood what he is coming for.
